questions.stem: A 10-week-old infant was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe bronchopneumonia requiring intubation and ventilation. She suffered repeated apneic attacks. She had been born at full term by normal vaginal delivery, with no instrumentation. Her APGAR scores had been 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes respectively. She had received her 8-week immunizations with DTaP/IPV/HiB, PCV , meningococcal B, and rotavirus vaccines 1 week before she became unwell. She lived at home with her parents, grandmother, and two older siblings. Initial investigations revealed a lymphocytosis.
questions.lead_in: What microbiological findings would be most consistent with this infection?

options.text: Bisected pearl colonies on charcoal cephalexin agar
Blue–grey colonies on Thayer Martin agar with vancomycin, colistin, nystatin
Grey colonies on Hoyle’s agar with potassium tellurite
Colonies on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with L cysteine which fluoresce yellow–green under UV light
Growth around combined X+V disc only on nutrient agar

questions.explanation: Bisected pearl colonies on charcoal cephalexin agar This would be consistent with Bordetella pertussis, the likely pathogen in this infant (see image). Perinasal swabs with a Dacron Tip or nasopharyngeal aspirates are the specimens of choice and should be plated at the bedside or placed in charcoal transport medium. PCR is more sensitive, especially later in the presentation and after antibiotics. The highest rates of disease in the UK are in infants under 3 months. It is highly contagious, with up to 90% of unimmunized household contacts developing the disease. Public health should be notified as contacts may need assessment, chemoprophylaxis, and vaccination (households with other infants <4 months old, pregnant women, and healthcare workers). (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q49

questions.question: Bordetella pertussis.
questions.model_answer: a) Nasopharyngeal specimen (posterior NP swab of calcium alginate/Dacron/rayon, or preferably NP aspirate) sent for nucleic acid amplification (PCR) is the diagnostic test of choice: PCR is more sensitive than culture, is rapid, distinguishes B. pertussis from B. holmesii/B. parapertussis, and remains positive later in the disease course. Culture (BG or RL medium) is the most specific test but insensitive (15-80%). Serology (anti-PT IgG ELISA, single-serum or paired) is useful in adolescents/adults presenting late when cultures are negative. DFA is rapid but has poor sensitivity/specificity and is no longer recommended for confirmation.

questions.question: Bordetella pertussis.
questions.model_answer: b) A macrolide is first-line. For adolescents and adults with suspected or proven pertussis within 21 days of symptom onset: azithromycin 500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg daily for the next 4 days (alternatives: clarithromycin 1000 mg/day in two divided doses for 7 days, or erythromycin 2000 mg/day in four divided doses for 7-14 days). Infants <1 month: azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day for 5 days (macrolide of choice given the erythromycin association with pyloric stenosis). Antibiotics eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage/limit transmission but do not clearly alter the clinical course once the paroxysmal stage is established; supportive care is paramount, especially in infants.

cohort_answer.text: Azithromycin 500mg x1st day then 250mg x4 days

questions.question: Bordetella pertussis.
questions.model_answer: c) Chemoprophylaxis (macrolide) is directed at close contacts of a case to prevent transmission. In the United States it is recommended for all household and other close contacts, including child care contacts. In Canada it is recommended for household contacts and for high-risk contacts, specifically infants and pregnant women in the third trimester. It is of greatest benefit in high-risk populations (e.g. infants <6 months) because randomized data show little clinical benefit in contacts >6 months of age.

cohort_answer.text: All household contacts (even if exposed person is fully immunized); Out of household contacts at high risk (e.g. infants <1 year, pregnant 3rd trimester)

questions.question: Bordetella pertussis.
questions.model_answer: d) Prophylaxis must be given early to be of benefit: it should be started early in the course of the index case's illness and before the first secondary case occurs. It is generally NOT recommended once 21 days have elapsed since the onset of cough in the index patient, because by then transmission has usually already occurred.

cohort_answer.text: Most effective if started within 21 days of onset of cough in the index patient
